label: Hyperbolic Geometry in the Cayley-Klein Picture
notes: Open by framing hyperbolic geometry as projective geometry plus a distinguished real conic, the absolute. Printed pages 505 through 524 collect selected topics: the disk models, cross-ratio distance, the angle defect, cycles, and isometries. Stress that every hyperbolic fact will be read off Euclidean-looking pictures whose measuring rule has quietly changed.

label: The Absolute Conic and Two Disk Models
notes: Contrast the two faces of the same Cayley-Klein metric. The Klein disk draws geodesics as straight chords but distorts angles; the Poincare disk bends geodesics into orthogonal arcs but keeps angles honest. Both live inside the absolute unit circle, and the model choice is just a choice of convenient coordinates on one hyperbolic plane.

label: Hyperbolic Distance as a Cross-Ratio
notes: Derive the metric the projective way. A line through two interior points meets the absolute in two ideal endpoints; the cross-ratio of the four points is a projective invariant, and its logarithm, halved, is the hyperbolic distance. Emphasize additivity along a line and the blow-up to infinity as either point slides toward the boundary.

label: Lines, Ideal Points, and Ultraparallels
notes: Classify how two hyperbolic lines can relate. Chords that cross inside are intersecting; chords sharing a boundary endpoint are asymptotic parallels; disjoint chords are ultraparallel. Make the projective punchline explicit: ultraparallel lines have a unique common perpendicular, found as the polar of their pole with respect to the absolute conic.

label: Triangles, Angle Sum, and the Defect
notes: State the signature hyperbolic theorem: a triangle's angles sum to strictly less than pi, and the missing amount, the defect, equals the area in the standard normalization. Walk through why this forbids similar-but-not-congruent triangles and why an ideal triangle with three boundary vertices attains the maximal area pi.

label: Hyperbolic Pythagoras and Thales
notes: Show that classical theorems survive only in corrected form. Right triangles obey a multiplicative law in cosh rather than an additive square law, and expanding sinh recovers the Euclidean version in the small-length limit. For Thales, polarity in the Klein disk sends a pencil of lines to a pencil, so the right-angle locus traces a conic.

label: Cycles: Circles, Horocycles, Hypercycles
notes: Catalogue the constant-curvature curves. A proper circle is the locus equidistant from an interior center; a horocycle is its limit with center pushed to a single ideal point; a hypercycle is the equidistant curve of a line. In the Poincare disk all three look like Euclidean circles or arcs, distinguished only by where the center sits relative to the absolute.

label: Isometries as Projective Automorphisms
notes: Define hyperbolic isometries as the projective transformations fixing the absolute conic, equivalently the disk-preserving Mobius maps. Classify them by fixed points: elliptic maps fix one interior point and rotate, parabolic maps fix one boundary point, and hyperbolic maps fix two boundary points and translate along the geodesic joining them.

label: Regular n-Gons and the Tiling Condition
notes: Turn angle freedom into construction. A regular n-gon with vertex angle two-pi-over-m splits into right triangles with angles pi-over-n and pi-over-m, and the circumradius is real exactly when one-over-n plus one-over-m is below one-half. Equality marks the Euclidean boundary case; strict inequality opens the whole catalogue of hyperbolic tilings.

label: Symmetry Orbits and Exponential Growth
notes: Read a tessellation as a group orbit, not decoration. Disk-preserving Mobius generators move points by genuine isometries even though Euclidean spacing collapses near the boundary. Emphasize that the area inside radius r grows like the hyperbolic cosine, so orbits and tilings expand exponentially, which is why so many regular tilings exist.

label: Worked Reading: Defect of a Disk Triangle
notes: Work a concrete defect computation. Place three vertices in the Poincare disk, draw the orthogonal-arc sides, measure the conformal Euclidean tangent angles, and subtract their sum from pi. The result is both the defect and the area; push one vertex toward the boundary and watch the angle shrink while the area climbs toward the ideal maximum.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: Close by collecting the throughline: one absolute conic generates distance by cross-ratio, area by defect, parallels by boundary contact, and symmetry by conic-preserving projectivities. Remind students that hyperbolic equalities relax into inequalities, leaving room for infinitely many tilings, and point ahead to the unified Cayley-Klein treatment of all three classical geometries.
